newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus says yes to hardline Lukashenko.
newsitem.headline: Belarus says yes to hardline Lukashenko.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko claimed a huge victory over parliament, the opposition and the highest court in Belarus on Monday after millions of voters gave him a mandate to seize sweeping powers.

"It will be very hard for my opponents to insist there were violations, that the referendum was illegal. The overwhelming majorities won by all the president's questions speak for themselves," a confident Lukashenko told a news conference.

More than 70 percent of the electorate backed Lukashenko's draft constitution on Sunday, allowing him to re-form parliament as two chambers, appoint half the constitutional court which opposes him and recommence his five-year term.
Lukashenko said he hoped to re-form the institutions by Christmas though the new constitution gives him two months.
It is unclear how parliament will be formed. Lukashenko says the deputies will approve the appointment of 110 of the existing 199 to a lower house and all but six of a 64-seat upper house.

Parliament is deeply divided between allies and foes of Lukashenko but the president insisted he would not need to call new elections, which the new constitution gives him the right to do if deputies cannot agree within a month.
"There will be consensus and harmony between president and parliament," he said, adding that a "concrete document" on the subject would be prepared within a few days.
There was also no mention by the central electoral commission, state television, or Lukashenko of the results of by-elections to 51 vacant seats in parliament.

Since winning the presidency by a landslide in July 1994, Lukashenko has become increasingly authoritarian, and the new constitution awards him powers over institutions which a Council of Europe analysis recently said "could not be stronger".

The population of 10 million has been subjected to an extremely one-sided campaign from state television and radio in the run-up to the referendum, in which they had to answer four questions proposed by the president and three by parliament.
Results showed Lukashenko winning all seven.
Viktor Gonchar, sacked by the president as the head of the electoral commission though he was appointed by parliament, told Reuters high turnout figures showed the results were faked.
"Even during the presidential campaign (in 1994), when political activity was at its highest, it was lower (than 84 percent). The figures are simply fantastic," he said.
Gonchar said the turnout in big towns had been particularly high during the last four hours of voting. "This would be understandable in summer, but not in late November," he said.
Parliament's draft constitution, which would have abolished the presidency and strengthened parliament, won the backing of just 7.9 percent of the electorate.
The electorate also voted to keep the death penalty, let Lukashenko appoint local leaders and ban a free market in land.
Semyon Sharetsky, the main opposition figure and parliament speaker, has led communists, agrarians, liberals and democrats who have been trying to remove Lukashenko from office.
Impeachment proceedings are due to resume on Tuesday but Lukashenko seemed confident that the case would lapse.
Lukashenko made clear that the 11 constitutional court judges would have a chance of being reappointed, but only if they stopped trying to block his decisions.

He urged more than 70 deputies who signed last week's impeachment papers to withdraw their signatures and said: "I think any resistance to the will of the people will, to put it mildly, be received negatively by the people".
Lukashenko, whose policies have isolated Belarus from international financial institutions, said he planned economic reforms.
The angular moustachioed leader also said he wanted Belarus to join the European Union -- a departure from his usual policy of looking only to Russia, with which he formed a "community."
"Belarus is a European state and it must be in the family of European states," he said. Diplomats say that as things stand, Belarus has no chance of joining the EU.
